newsitem.title: SPAIN: Truce in battle for Spain's digital TV platform.
newsitem.headline: Truce in battle for Spain's digital TV platform.

text.p: A truce appeared on Wednesday in a complex industry battle in Spain over the establishment of a digital television platform after the ruling Popular Party (PP) changed contested parts of a proposed TV law.

The PP, which backs a universal system called multicrypt to decode pay TV signals, proposed an amendment allowing the use of another decoder type called simulcrypt after hours of negotiation in a parliamentary committee.

The minority PP government, which proposed the change after losing support on the issue from a key parliamentary ally, denied that it had reversed positions or even that there was a struggle for control of Spain's underdeveloped pay TV market.

"The change is that if there is an agreement on another system and it's fully compatible, it can be used. If not, multicrypt, the system preferred by the PP will be used," PP deputy Ana Mato told Reuters on Wednesday.
The government's former insistence on the multicrypt system had angered CanalSatelite, which had already launched a platform for digital television based on simulcrypt decoders.
The government says it prefers multicrypt because consumers can use the unscrambler for any digital platform, whereas simulcrypt is reportedly not fully interchangeable.

The decoders are devices that consumers buy or rent from the digital television provider to unscramble its programming protection -- usually encrypted TV signals that make the screen appear fuzzy -- and provide a clear picture.

CanalSatelite complained last month to Europe's competition commission that the Spanish government was abusing its power by introducing regulatory obstacles to favour a rival digital platform that has participation from state-owned companies.
The group said it was satisfied with the new draft regulation on decoders.
"We always knew that our decoders were compatible and complied with the requirements," a spokeswoman for Sogecable, the lead partner in CanalSatelite, told Reuters on Wednesday.
But she said the group was surprised at another new clause approved in parliament on Tuesday that limited a company's stake in a digital television provider to 25 percent.
"It's an attempt to put up another obstacle to the working of our platform," the Sogecable spokeswoman said, adding that in practice the group could reorganise its statutes to comply.

CanalSatelite is 15 percent owned by commerical channel Antena 3 and 85 percent owned by Sogecable, which is in turn 25 percent owned by France's Canal Plus and 25 percent owned by Spanish media group Prisa.
The group, which has links to the leading opposition Socialist party, is the only platform operating at the moment with 9,000 clients since its launch in January and a waiting list of 19,000.

The other digital platform is led by the recently privatised telecoms operator Telefonica with participation from the state's Radio and Television of Spain (RTVE) and Mexico's Televisa. It will use state-owned satellite Hispasat.
Telefonica had no comment on the new draft law.
